contributions.title: Curriculum Embedding Lab — Embed AI in Your Course
contributions.summary: A 90-minute faculty lab whose deliverable is a decision, not a demo. Each participant builds a working, discipline-grounded AI tool from a persona matched to their field, then writes a curriculum plan for where it belongs in a course they actually teach — and, explicitly, where it does not. Ships with a student-facing companion notebook (Quiz Me, Socratic Hint, Explain-Back) and six licence-clean discipline personas.

learning_outcomes: Identify where in a specific course an AI tool adds instructional value, and articulate what the instructor still does.
Build a discipline-grounded AI tool from a persona brief, using retrieval over a real document from the field.
State an explicit boundary for where AI does not belong in one's own teaching, and defend it.
Commit to one dated, specific instructional action.

knowledge: No coding experience required; participants run about five cells of Python.
accounts: AWS account with Amazon SageMaker Studio access
Amazon Bedrock model access for Amazon Nova Lite in the session region
prerequisites.expected_cost: Under USD 1 per participant in Bedrock inference. SageMaker Studio compute is billed for the duration of the session and should be shut down afterward.

In about 15 minutes participants build a grounded, source-citing AI tutor for their own field and see directly what grounding buys them, because the notebook asks the same question with and without the source document. Ships in two paths — free Google Colab plus Hugging Face, or SageMaker Studio plus Bedrock — so faculty keep a working copy after cloud access ends.

Build a tutor that answers only from a supplied document and cites the passage it used.

contributions.title: Class Participation Scoring — Transcript to Draft Score
contributions.summary: Point this notebook at a Zoom transcript of one class meeting and the material you covered that day. It identifies who spoke, judges what they talked about against your embedded lesson rather than the model's own knowledge, and drafts a 0–4 participation score per student with the evidence behind it. The output is a draft a human reviews, never a grade the tool assigns on its own.

intended_use.description: Drafts class-participation scores for a discussion-based course from a recorded class transcript, so an instructor reviews evidence-backed drafts instead of scoring from memory. Each score combines quantity, topical relevance judged against the day's embedded lesson material, and substance. Requires instructor review before any score is recorded.
learning_outcomes: Ground a relevance judgment in supplied course material rather than model priors.
Review and override AI-drafted scores using the evidence attached to each one.
Apply institutional policy on class recording and student records before using real transcripts.

knowledge: Comfort running cells in a notebook.
Institutional clearance to use class recordings and transcripts, with students notified. FERPA in the US, or the local equivalent.

contributions.title: Paper Autograder — Rubric-Based Draft Grading
contributions.summary: Point this notebook at your course material, a grading rubric, and a folder of student papers. For each paper it scores every rubric criterion, backs each score with verbatim quotes, computes the weighted grade in code rather than in the model, and drafts separate notes for the instructor and for the student. Runs on Bedrock or fully local via Ollama, where nothing leaves the machine.

intended_use.description: Drafts rubric-based grades for written work. Criteria about using course concepts correctly are judged only against the instructor's embedded material, so a confident, well-written paper that misuses the concepts scores lower rather than higher. The overall grade is computed in code from tiers and criterion weights. This is not a plagiarism or AI-writing detector and must never inform an academic-integrity decision.
learning_outcomes: Express a grading rubric in a machine-readable form with explicit criterion weights.
Distinguish fluent writing from correct reasoning when reviewing drafted grades.
Review evidence-backed drafts and override them before recording any grade.

knowledge: Comfort running cells in a notebook.
Institutional clearance to process student papers. FERPA in the US, or the local equivalent. The Ollama path keeps papers on the local machine.

contributions.title: The Assignment Lifecycle — Quick Assessment Demo Session
contributions.summary: A 90-minute facilitated session that walks a room through one assignment's full lifecycle — write the rubric, stress-test it, grade against it, and triage submissions before the deadline. Built around a single fluent, confident, and wrong student paper that earns a B+ under a vague rubric and an F under a rubric that names what correct means. contributions.title: Build and Evaluate an AI Marketing Assistant in PartyRock
contributions.summary: A no-code assignment in which students build a working marketing-content app in Amazon PartyRock, then run one identical scenario through three prompt strategies — bare, role plus context, and fully structured — and score the three outputs against the same five criteria. The app is the hook; the comparison table is the assignment. Built for a mixed-major audience with no programming background.

learning_outcomes: Build a functioning generative-AI application without writing code.
Reference app inputs inside a prompt so that outputs change with user input.
Compare a bare prompt, a role-and-context prompt, and a structured prompt on one identical scenario.
Score generative-AI output against relevance, specificity, tone, completeness, and usability rather than accepting it at face value.
Explain which prompt elements — role, context, tone, constraints, output format — most changed the result, citing their own outputs.

knowledge: None. No programming background is assumed of students or instructor.
Students should be able to describe a product or service in a few sentences.
accounts: A free PartyRock sign-in via an Apple, Google, or Amazon account. No AWS account or credit card is required.

contributions.title: Build, Break, and Question a PartyRock Phishing Detector
contributions.summary: Students build a phishing-email classifier in Amazon PartyRock, classify at least 15 emails themselves before the AI sees them, then compare both against instructor-held ground truth. The assignment then inverts: students spend a round trying to fool the detector they just built, log every technique, and write up where a confident-sounding verdict should not be trusted. No code, and the reflection is worth more than the build.

learning_outcomes: Build a functioning AI-powered classification tool without writing code.
Compare human judgment against AI judgment on the same task, using a labelled dataset.
Design adversarial test cases that probe the limits of an AI system.
Judge whether a model's stated confidence tracks its actual correctness.
Articulate, in writing, where AI helps, where it fails, and why human review still matters in security workflows.

knowledge: None for students. No programming background is assumed.

INSTRUCTOR: you must supply a ground-truth bank of at least 15 pre-labelled sample emails before this can run. Roughly 40% clearly phishing, 30% clearly legitimate, 30% genuinely ambiguous. Build it from vetted phishing-awareness archives or institutional security training material, never from real captured personal mail. See the facilitation guide.

contributions.title: Fundamentals of AI Literacy
contributions.summary: A self-paced, non-credit online course that introduces AI to people who will never build one — new students, faculty, and staff. Three video modules with quizzes carry the vocabulary, from machine learning through agentic AI, and a final project makes it concrete: students write one structured prompt about careers in their own major, run it unchanged through PartyRock, ChatGPT, and Copilot, and defend which answer was best. contributions.title: Project O.R.A.C.L.E. — A GenAI-Enhanced International Relations Lab
contributions.summary: A 1-credit lab module that gives International Relations students the hands-on research laboratory their STEM peers already have. A fictional 2025 alien-contact scenario casts students as "non-expert but educated analysts" and scaffolds them from finding where AI fails in Lab 1 to building a PartyRock app that works around those limits in Lab 2. The target it is built against is fluent-but-shallow AI output, and it closes with a one-on-one oral defense where students justify their research design and their AI use in person.

learning_outcomes: Apply IR theories and approaches to a focused question concerning an extraterrestrial encounter.
Develop and communicate a research design that reflects academic reasoning, data–method fit, and awareness of bias.
Describe the basic functions of general LLMs and express their limitations for academic work.
Use GenAI tools ethically to support idea generation, literature identification, and clarity, and document that use.
Evaluate the strengths and limitations of GenAI's role in social-science research.
Reflect on the utility of GenAI in their academic, professional, or personal futures.

contributions.title: Assignment Defender — AI-Proofing Assistant
contributions.summary: A published Amazon Quick app that reads an assignment's goals, instructions, and rubric, then estimates how well generative AI could satisfy it on its own. Faculty set the maximum grade they think an AI-only submission should earn, and the app returns an AI Robustness Score, a SWOT analysis, and three redesign options at increasing strength. The goal is not to block AI but to find where it substitutes for the skill actually being assessed. No account or coding needed to use it.

intended_use.description: A formative instructional-design and decision-support tool for faculty redesigning an assessment. It takes assignment goals, learning objectives, instructions, and grading criteria, plus a faculty-set ceiling for what an AI-only submission should be able to earn, and returns an AI Robustness Score, a SWOT review, and three redesign options — Minimum Robustness, Heightened Security, and Best Fit. It does not make an assignment AI-proof and it does not detect AI use; it identifies where AI can substitute for the skill being assessed so a human can decide what to change. Every recommendation is a draft for faculty judgment, to be checked against course outcomes, accessibility needs, disciplinary expectations, workload, and institutional policy before adoption.
learning_outcomes: Identify which parts of an existing assignment generative AI could satisfy without the student demonstrating the target skill.
Set and defend a deliberate ceiling for what an AI-only submission should be able to earn.
Rewrite rubric criteria so that credit depends on evidence AI cannot supply, such as named personal experience or exact figures from an attached dataset.
Distinguish assessment redesign from AI detection, and explain why the first is durable and the second is not.
